summary: An excerpt from a science-fiction novel (Book 15, part 152) in which Ray explains to Becker how he isolated the signature of a suspect, Freddy, and used the surveillance net to track his movements. The footage shows a gap around the time of death, while days of tracking place Freddy at a high-class, exclusive franchise near the main lift. Ray says the pattern is a start toward a circumstantial case, but Becker says it is not enough to bring in a powerful Whiston for questioning.
one_line: In a shipboard science-fiction excerpt, Ray uses surveillance footage to show suspect Freddy's whereabouts, but Becker wants stronger proof before questioning a powerful Whiston.
key_facts: Ray says he used roundabout methods to get a rat near the Whiston suite so he could isolate Freddy's signature.
Ray says he spent time in the presence of Miss Whiston while gathering evidence, which he describes as the official record.
Ray coded a search of the surveillance net into the regular drone routine after isolating Freddy's signature.
Ray redirected the surveillance net to track Freddy's movements for the last four days.
The footage shows conclusive movements before the estimated time of death and activities a few hours after, with a big gaping hole in the middle.
Becker reacts to the gap in the footage with the words "Aw, hell."
Freddy is found at a franchise described as high class, high price, with exclusive tastes, where lap dances in the back room are cheaper than the drinks.
The franchise is right off the main lift, giving customers easy access to just about anywhere on the ship.
Freddy lines up in the nightly batch transmission queue like other businessmen, the only time he is not at the franchise.
Ray cut footage of Freddy's less liquid adventures because it was not family friendly and the stream might be played at various venues.
Freddy's passenger pre-screen shows no psychological issues, no legal history, and no profile as a potential incident perpetrator.
Ray says Freddy has no reputation for violence, though he is said to be violent where his sister is concerned.
Becker says there is no definitive proof, only evidence of absence during the critical hours.
Ray responds that he has pattern, which is the start of a decent circumstantial case.
Becker feels it is not enough to bring in a Whiston for questioning, since the family is powerful in this corner of human space.
